items.stem: In an evacuated parallel-plate velocity-calibration gap, an initially stationary singly charged potassium ion (m = 6.49 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, q = +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) accelerates across a uniform electric field between parallel plates 0.055 m apart with potential difference 2200 V. Neglecting gravity, what speed does the singly charged potassium ion reach upon arriving at the 0 V plate?
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2200 / 6.49 × 10⁻²⁶) = 1.04 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (B).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 1.04 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Inside an electrostatic aerosol-charging test section, two like-sign point charges of +7 nC and +3 nC are fixed 0.7 m apart, with +7 nC on the left. Point P lies on the connecting axis 0.3 m from the left charge. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² throughout.
items.workedSolution: (a) Both positive sources repel a positive test charge placed at P, so the left charge pushes rightward while the right charge pushes leftward. (b) |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.3)² = 699 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.4)² = 169 N C⁻¹. Subtracting the opposing vectors yields 531 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: States that a positive test charge between like-sign sources experiences opposite forces from the left and right charges.
Evaluates E = k|q|/r² at r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.4 m.
Subtracts the two opposing field magnitudes.
Obtains 531 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Within a shielded Faraday enclosure used for sensor testing, along the 1 m line segment between +4 nC (left) and −16 nC (right), point P sits 0.2 m from the left source. Model the charges in free space (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²), taking V = 0 at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = k(4 × 10⁻⁹/0.2 + -16 × 10⁻⁹/0.8) = 0 V. (b) At P both fields point to the right, giving E = 899 N C⁻¹ + 225 N C⁻¹ = 1.12 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes signed charges with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.8 m into V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = 0 V.
Applies inverse-square law E = k|q|/r² to both sources.
Adds the two collinear field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.12 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Between the flat brass electrodes of a Millikan electrostatic cell, a uniform electrostatic gap of width 0.025 m operates with 150 V across its parallel plates while a carrier (q = +4 × 10⁻⁸ C, m = 4 × 10⁻⁶ kg) traverses from the high-potential plate to the 0 V plate. Neglect edge effects and gravitational forces.
items.workedSolution: (a) Uniform field E = V / d = 150 / 0.025 = 6.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹. (b) Work done by the field W = qV = (4 × 10⁻⁸)(150) = 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ J.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes V = 150 V and d = 0.025 m into E = V / d.
Obtains 6.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹.
Applies W = qV (or W = qEd).
Obtains 6.00 × 10⁻⁶ J.

items.stem: Along a precision dielectric guide rail, three uniform-field equipotential lines are spaced evenly with potentials 340 V, 200 V, and 60 V from left to right separated by 0.035 m between neighbouring lines. A charged dielectric bead carrying +2 × 10⁻⁸ C and mass 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ kg is released at rest on the 200 V line along a horizontal frictionless axis.
items.workedSolution: (a) E = (200 − 60) / 0.035 = 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right. (b) a = qE / m = 5.71 m s⁻². (c) Using ½mv² = q(140), v = 0.632 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides adjacent potential step by spacing s.
Obtains 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right.
Applies a = qE / m.
Obtains 5.71 m s⁻².
Equates ½mv² = q(140) or uses v² = 2as.
Obtains 0.632 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Along a horizontal ceramic support rod in free space, two stationary charges of −4 nC on the left and −8 nC on the right have separation 0.6 m, with point P marked 0.2 m from the left source. With zero potential set at infinity in vacuum, use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the electric potential at point P?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.4 m. Thus V = −180 V + (−180 V) = −360 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.2 + kq₂/0.4 = −360 V (C).

items.stem: Across the measurement track of a non-contact Kelvin probe bench, two fixed point charges of −10 nC (left) and +5 nC (right) are held 0.75 m apart. Point P lies on the straight line joining them at a distance of 0.25 m to the right of the −10 nC charge. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² for free-space electrostatic interactions.
items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the left (toward the negative left source and away from the positive right source), so they reinforce toward the left. (b) With r₁ = 0.25 m and r₂ = 0.5 m, |E₁| = 1.44 × 10³ N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 180 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 1.62 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Explains using a positive test charge that both source fields at P act in the same direction.
Applies E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.25 m and r₂ = 0.5 m.
Adds the two collinear field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.62 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

parts.prompt: State and explain why the two individual electric field contributions reinforce rather than oppose each other at point P.
parts.expectedAnswer: Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the left (toward the negative left source and away from the positive right source), so they reinforce toward the left.
workingSteps: Electric field direction is the force direction on a positive test charge.
Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the left (toward the negative left source and away from the positive right source), so they reinforce toward the left.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and state the direction of the resultant electric field at point P.
workingSteps: |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 1.44 × 10³ N C⁻¹; |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 180 N C⁻¹.
Resultant E = |E₁| + |E₂| = 1.62 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.stem: Inside a cryogenic linear Paul-trap alignment fixture, point sources +9 nC at x = 0 and −6 nC at x = 0.7 m remain fixed while a small probe of charge −1.8 nC is placed at x = 0.3 m (point P). Assume vacuum (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) and reference all scalar potentials to zero at infinity. What is the electric potential at P due to the two fixed source charges?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 270 V + (−135 V) = 135 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.4) = 135 V (C), independent of q_test.

items.stem: In a dry-nitrogen micro-electrostatics apparatus, two collinear point charges of +12 nC (left) and −4 nC (right) are separated by 0.4 m. Point P lies outside the pair to the right of both charges, at a total distance of 0.8 m from the left-hand +12 nC charge. Assume vacuum permittivity such that k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at exterior point P?
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.8 m to the right of +12 nC and r₂ = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 m to the right of −4 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 56.2 N C⁻¹ to the left (A).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.8 m and r₂ = 0.4 m to obtain 56.2 N C⁻¹ to the left (A).

items.stem: On a sapphire isolation substrate inside a cleanroom vacuum stage, along a 0.9 m baseline in free space, a +2 nC point charge is fixed at the left end and a +8 nC point charge is fixed at the right end. At what distance from the +2 nC charge along the line joining the charges is the resultant electric field equal to zero?
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.9 − x)², so (0.9 − x)/x = √(8/2). Solving yields x = 0.9 × √2/(√2 + √8) = 0.300 m (C).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.9 − x)² to obtain x = 0.300 m (C).

items.stem: Along a horizontal ceramic support rod in free space, along a 0.7 m vacuum baseline between fixed charges +10 nC on the left and +3 nC on the right, point P is marked 0.3 m from +10 nC. A small probe charge of −3 nC is placed at P without disturbing the fixed sources. Take the Coulomb constant as k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electrostatic force acting on the −3 nC probe charge?
items.workedSolution: At P (r₁ = 0.3 m, r₂ = 0.4 m), the resultant electric field is E = 830 N C⁻¹ to the right. Multiplying by q_test = −3 nC gives F = q_test E = 2.49 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates E = 830 N C⁻¹ and F = qE = 2.49 × 10⁻⁶ N to the left (B).

items.stem: Across the central region of a wide guard-ring capacitor, three vertical equipotential lines are drawn at 280 V (left), 140 V (middle), and 0 V (right), with adjacent lines separated by 0.035 m. A particle of charge +3.5 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the 280 V line to the 0 V line.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = q(V_final − V_initial) with ΔV = -280 V.
Obtains ΔE_p = −9.80 × 10⁻⁶ J (with correct sign).
Applies W_field = −ΔE_p = q(V_initial − V_final).
Obtains W_field = 9.80 × 10⁻⁶ J (with correct sign).

items.stem: Across a heavy-ion electrostatic stopping-distance calculation, a projectile triply charged lithium nucleus of charge +3e approaches head-on a stationary gold nucleus of atomic number Z = 79 (charge +79e) to a distance of closest approach r_min = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. What is the electric potential due to the gold nucleus at distance r_min?
items.workedSolution: Radial potential of the +79e nucleus is V = kZe / r_min = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 79 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.07 × 10⁶ V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = kZe / r_min = 2.07 × 10⁶ V (C).

items.stem: Along a straight dielectric mounting rod inside an evacuated bell jar, positive point sources +4 nC at x = 0 and +36 nC at x = 0.8 m are mounted along a straight insulating bar. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and define electric potential to be zero at infinity. What is the electric potential at the unique point on the line between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero?
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.8 × √4/(√4 + √36) = 0.200 m from +4 nC (and 0.600 m from +36 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 719 V (B).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.200 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 719 V (B).

items.stem: In a Millikan chamber ($g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, air viscosity $\eta = 1.81 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa s}$), an oil droplet of density 880 kg m⁻³ falls at a terminal speed of 1.10 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ with the electric field off, and is held stationary by 717 V across plates separated by 12.0 mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) $r = 1.02 μm$. (b) $m = 3.90 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg$. (c) $Q = 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$, which is 4.0 excess electrons.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $6\pi\eta r v = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho g$ with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Correct radius 1.02 μm.
Applies $m = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho$.
Correct mass 3.90 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg.
Uses $Q = mgd / V$ with $d = 0.0120\text{ m}$.
Correct charge 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Divides by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ to conclude 4.0 excess electrons.

items.stem: Across the test region of a high-impedance electrometer bench, on a straight vacuum baseline of total length 3 x between +8Q on the left and +5Q on the right, point P lies 2 x from the left source. Write the resultant electric field magnitude at P in the form E = α kQ/x², where k is the Coulomb constant.
items.workedSolution: (a) The right positive charge produces a larger repulsive field magnitude at P than the left positive charge, so the net electric field points to the left. (b) α = |8/2² − 5/1²| = |2.00 − 5.00| = 3.00.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant direction as to the left with valid reasoning.
Forms inverse-square terms 8/2² and 5/1².
Subtracts the opposing dimensionless field coefficients.
Obtains α = 3.00.

items.stem: Within a dust-plasma levitation chamber evacuated to low pressure, along a 0.6 m vacuum baseline with q₁ = 4 × 10⁻⁹ C at the left end and q₂ at the right end, the net electric field is zero at a point 0.2 m from q₁.
items.workedSolution: (a) q₁ and q₂ have the same sign so their fields oppose between them. (b) |q₂/q₁| = ((0.6 − 0.2)/0.2)² = (0.4/0.2)² = 4.00. (c) q₂ = +(4.00)(4 × 10⁻⁹ C) = +1.60 × 10⁻⁸ C.

markScheme.criterion: States same sign because fields must oppose in the region between the charges.
Uses |q₂/q₁| = ((d − x₀)/x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.4 m.
Obtains 4.00.
Multiplies q₁ by ratio from (b) with positive sign.
Obtains q₂ = +1.60 × 10⁻⁸ C.

parts.prompt: State whether q₁ and q₂ have the same sign or opposite signs, explaining your reasoning.
parts.expectedAnswer: They have the same sign because their individual electric field vectors must point in opposite directions to cancel between the charges.
workingSteps: Opposite-sign charges produce fields in the same direction everywhere between them.
Therefore q₁ and q₂ must have the same sign.

parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio |q₂ / q₁|.
workingSteps: Distance from q₂ to null point = 0.6 − 0.2 = 0.4 m.

parts.prompt: Hence determine the signed value of q₂.
workingSteps: q₂ is positive (same sign as q₁) with magnitude 4.00 × 4 × 10⁻⁹ C.

items.stem: Between two large parallel charged plates separated by a small gap, equipotential lines drawn at equal voltage intervals are parallel and equally spaced. What does this uniform spacing show?
items.workedSolution: Since field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field, equal spacing corresponds to a constant field strength. Therefore the correct statement is: It shows constant uniform electric field because field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows electric potential is identical everywhere between the two plates.
options.distractorRationale: Potential varies linearly from one plate to the other; only the gradient is constant.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows electric field strength falls off as inverse distance squared from the positive plate.
options.distractorRationale: Equal equipotential spacing implies constant E = V/d, not 1/r² decay.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows zero electrostatic force acts on an electron placed midway between the plates.
options.distractorRationale: A constant non-zero field exerts a constant force F = qE.

items.stem: A laboratory parallel-plate capacitor with air between its plates is charged to 18.0 V and disconnected from the supply before inserting a polar mica slab (εᵣ = 4.50). The overlapping plate area is 180 cm², plate separation is 1.20 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 597 pF. (b) 4.00 V. (c) E' = 4.78 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI units in C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d.
Calculates C' = 597 pF.
Recognises isolated Q is constant so V' = V₀ / εᵣ.
Obtains 4.00 V.
Calculates final stored energy E' = 4.78 nJ.
States polar molecules rotate so negative ends face the positive plate.

Explains opposing internal field lowers net field and raises capacitance (polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity).

items.stem: Why is gravitational potential at every finite distance from a planet always negative, whereas electric potential around an isolated charged sphere can be either positive or negative?
items.workedSolution: Both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential. Therefore the correct statement is: Taking zero potential at infinity, both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential

options.label: A
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, gravitational potential is defined at the centre of Earth rather than at infinity.
options.distractorRationale: Both radial gravitational and radial electric potentials define zero at infinity.

options.label: B
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, gravity is weaker than magnetism so its potential is assigned a negative label arbitrarily.
options.distractorRationale: The negative sign follows physically from doing positive external work to separate attractive masses to infinity.

options.label: C
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential

options.label: D
options.text: Taking zero potential at infinity, electric charges cannot attract each other so electric potential is always positive.
options.distractorRationale: Unlike charges attract, giving negative electric potential around a negative source charge.

items.stem: In a hydrogen atom, a proton (1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) and an electron (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg), each of charge magnitude 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, are 5.30 × 10⁻¹¹ m apart. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the ratio F_e / F_g.
items.workedSolution: F_e / F_g = e² / (4πε₀ G m_p m_e) = 2.26 × 10³⁹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds proton-electron force ratio 2.26 × 10³⁹.

items.stem: An electronics student charges an air-gap capacitor from a constant-voltage DC source through a resistor R, then slides a polar polymer dielectric slab (εᵣ > 1) into the gap while keeping the battery attached.
items.workedSolution: battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value. When charging from 0 to Q at fixed supply emf V, the battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value (a larger R slows current so charging takes longer, keeping ∫I²R dt = ½QV unchanged). Sliding the polar polymer into the gap causes its permanent molecular dipoles to rotate so negative ends face the positive plate and positive ends face the negative plate. These aligned dipoles set up an opposing internal electric field that tends to reduce the net field and plate potential difference; because the battery holds V constant across the plates, extra charge flows onto the plates until net field returns to V/d, raising C by εᵣ and increasing stored energy E = ½CV² by factor εᵣ.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States that the constant-emf battery transfers total work W = QV while the capacitor stores E = ½QV (area under linear V–Q graph).
L1b: Concludes that exactly 50% (½QV) is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of the value of R.
L2a: Explains that polar polymer molecules rotate to align their negative ends toward the positive plate and positive ends toward the negative plate.
L2b: States that aligned dipoles create an opposing internal electric field inside the slab.
L3a: Explains that because the battery maintains fixed potential difference V, additional charge flows from the supply onto the plates to restore V = Ed.
L3b: Concludes that Q, capacitance C = ε₀εᵣA/d, and stored energy E = ½CV² all increase by factor εᵣ.

parts.prompt: Explain why half the energy supplied during the initial charging stage is always lost as thermal energy regardless of R, then explain microscopically why inserting the polar polymer causes additional current to flow from the battery and increases the stored electrical energy.
parts.expectedAnswer: battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value. When charging from 0 to Q at fixed supply emf V, the battery supplies energy Q V while the capacitor stores half Q V so exactly fifty percent is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of resistance value (a larger R slows current so charging takes longer, keeping ∫I²R dt = ½QV unchanged). Sliding the polar polymer into the gap causes its permanent molecular dipoles to rotate so negative ends face the positive plate and positive ends face the negative plate. These aligned dipoles set up an opposing internal electric field that tends to reduce the net field and plate potential difference; because the battery holds V constant across the plates, extra charge flows onto the plates until net field returns to V/d, raising C by εᵣ and increasing stored energy E = ½CV² by factor εᵣ.
workingSteps: Explain 50% thermal loss via battery work QV vs triangular stored energy ½QV, independent of R.
Describe dipole alignment (− toward + plate) and opposing internal field.
Show why constant V draws additional charge from the battery, increasing C and stored energy by εᵣ.

items.stem: The side-by-side diagrams illustrate radial field lines and concentric dashed equipotentials surrounding a spherical planet of mass M and an isolated positive point charge +Q.
items.workedSolution: both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential. Both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential. Gravitational field strength g = F/m = GM/r² acts radially inward toward mass M, whereas electric field strength E = F/Q = Q/(4πε₀r²) acts outward from +Q (inward toward −Q). In both fields, field strength equals negative potential gradient (g = −ΔV/Δr, E = −ΔV/Δr), equipotential surfaces are concentric spheres everywhere perpendicular to field lines, closer equipotentials indicate a stronger field, and zero work is done moving along an equipotential. Between subatomic particles such as two protons, electrostatic force exceeds gravitational force by ~10³⁶, while electric fields can be shielded by conductors whereas gravitational fields cannot.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States both radial fields follow inverse-square laws (F ∝ 1/r², field ∝ 1/r²) with radial field lines and potential defined as zero at infinity.
L1b: States gravitational force acts on mass and is always attractive, whereas electric force acts on charge and can be attractive or repulsive.
L2a: Contrasts potential signs: gravitational potential V_g = −GM/r is always negative, while electric potential V_e = Q/(4πε₀r) is positive for +Q and negative for −Q.
L2b: States field strength equals the negative potential gradient (−ΔV/Δr) in both fields, so closely spaced equipotentials denote stronger fields.
L3a: Explains that equipotential surfaces intersect field lines at 90° and zero work is done moving a test mass or charge along an equipotential (ΔW = 0).
L3b: Notes the vast strength disparity at atomic scales (F_e/F_g ~ 10³⁶ for protons) and that electric fields can be shielded whereas gravitational fields cannot.

items.stem: Inside a university physics Van de Graaff calibration tunnel, two like-sign point charges of −8 nC and −4 nC are fixed 0.8 m apart, with −8 nC on the left. Point P lies on the connecting axis 0.3 m from the left charge. Assume vacuum permittivity such that k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field at P.
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.3)² = 799 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.5)² = 144 N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 655 N C⁻¹ directed to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 655 N C⁻¹ to the left (C).

items.stem: Along a horizontal ceramic support rod in free space, two opposite-sign sources of +3 nC on the left and −6 nC on the right have separation 0.6 m; axial point P is situated 0.2 m from +3 nC. Adopt k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electrostatic potential at infinite distance. Although the electric potential at P is zero, what is the resultant electric field at P?
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the right: E = 674 N C⁻¹ + 337 N C⁻¹ = 1.01 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (C).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and sums collinear contributions to obtain 1.01 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (C).

items.stem: Within a cleanroom charged-microparticle levitation cell, flat parallel plates spaced 0.025 m apart establish a 1000 V potential drop as a micro-carrier (mass 2.8 × 10⁻⁶ kg, charge +1.4 × 10⁻⁸ C) moves from the positive plate to the earthed 0 V plate. What kinetic energy (in joules) is transferred to the carrier by the electric field across the 1000 V potential drop?
items.workedSolution: Electrical work done across the full potential difference is W = qΔV = (1.4 × 10⁻⁸)(1000) = 1.40 × 10⁻⁵ J (B).

items.stem: Between wide planar electrodes in a vacuum tank, three parallel equipotential contours are marked labelled 500 V, 300 V, and 100 V from left to right at uniform spacing 0.05 m. Released from rest on the 300 V middle equipotential, a Millikan oil micro-droplet (m = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ kg, q = +0 C) accelerates horizontally across one spacing to the 100 V line. What is the magnitude of the horizontal electrostatic acceleration of the Millikan oil micro-droplet?

markScheme.criterion: Finds E = 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ and a = qE/m = 20.0 m s⁻² (A).

items.stem: Along a straight dielectric mounting rod inside an evacuated bell jar, two stationary charges of +5 nC on the left and +7 nC on the right have separation 0.6 m, with point P marked 0.2 m from the left source. With zero potential set at infinity in vacuum, use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Scalar potential V = k(q₁/0.2 + q₂/0.4) = 382 V. (b) Vector electric field E = 730 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Applies signed scalar sum V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = 382 V (including sign if negative).
Uses inverse-square magnitudes at r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.4 m.
Combines the two collinear field vectors with proper directions.
Obtains 730 N C⁻¹ to the right.

Calculate the magnitude and state the direction of the resultant electric field at point P.

items.stem: Why is the relative permittivity εᵣ of any insulating polar dielectric slab always greater than unity?
items.workedSolution: Polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity. Therefore the correct statement is: Because in an applied field, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

options.label: A
options.text: Because polar molecules permanently amplify the electric field between the plates above the vacuum value.
options.distractorRationale: Aligned dipoles oppose rather than reinforce the applied field.

options.label: B
options.text: Because polar molecules increase the plate separation d inside the capacitor.
options.distractorRationale: Plate separation d is fixed by geometry.

options.label: C
options.text: Because in an applied field, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity

options.label: D
options.text: Because free ions inside the insulator carry current straight from the positive plate to the negative plate.
options.distractorRationale: A dielectric is an insulator whose dipoles rotate in place without conducting through the gap.

items.stem: Along a horizontal ceramic support rod in free space, a point charge of −2 nC is fixed at x = 0 and a second point charge of +6 nC is fixed at x = 0.4 m. A field sensor is placed at point P on the axis at x = 0.15 m. Adopt the free-space constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Determine the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at point P.
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the left. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 799 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 863 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.25 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.66 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.66 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (D).

items.stem: Across the measurement track of a non-contact Kelvin probe bench, point sources +5 nC at x = 0 and +11 nC at x = 0.8 m remain fixed while a small probe of charge −2.6 nC is placed at x = 0.3 m (point P). Adopt k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electrostatic potential at infinite distance.
items.workedSolution: (a) E = 104 N C⁻¹ to the right. (b) Scalar sum V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.5) = 348 V. (c) Force on probe F = q_test E = 2.70 × 10⁻⁷ N to the left.

Obtains 2.70 × 10⁻⁷ N to the left.

items.stem: Along a horizontal ceramic support rod in free space, fixed sources −10 nC (left) and +2 nC (right) have separation 0.5 m. Observation point P is positioned on the extended axis beyond the right-hand charge, 0.7 m from −10 nC. Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² for free-space electrostatic interactions.
items.workedSolution: (a) Because P lies to the right of both opposite-sign charges, one source repels a positive test charge rightward while the other attracts it leftward, so their fields oppose. (b) Using r₁ = 0.7 m and r₂ = 0.2 m, |E₁| = 183 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 449 N C⁻¹, giving resultant E = 266 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: States opposite directions with correct test-charge reasoning.
Identifies r₁ = 0.7 m and r₂ = 0.2 m.
Applies signed vector superposition kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂².
Obtains 266 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: In a dry-nitrogen micro-electrostatics apparatus, along a 0.6 m baseline in free space, a +16 nC point charge is fixed at the left end and a +4 nC point charge is fixed at the right end.
items.workedSolution: (a) Between two positive charges their repulsive fields act in opposite directions, and equal field magnitudes require a smaller distance from the weaker right-hand charge. (b) Setting 16/x² = 4/(0.6 − x)² gives (0.6 − x)/x = √(4/16), hence x = 0.400 m.

markScheme.criterion: Explains opposing fields between positive sources and identifies closer proximity to the right-hand charge.
Equates inverse-square field magnitudes 16/x² = 4/(0.6 − x)².
Takes square roots correctly to linearize for x.
Obtains x = 0.400 m.

items.stem: Modelling a head-on nuclear collision below the fusion threshold, a projectile alpha particle of charge +2e approaches head-on a stationary zinc nucleus of atomic number Z = 30 (charge +30e) to a distance of closest approach r_min = 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Obtains 4.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Divides joule energy by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ (or multiplies V in volts by z).
Obtains 2.88 × 10⁶ eV.

Obtains V = 485 V.
States 0 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: A negatively charged oil droplet is held stationary between horizontal plates (top plate positive) when a brief burst of X-rays knocks one electron off the droplet. What happens and how must the plate voltage be adjusted to restore equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: Because $QV/d = mg$, losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required to hold the droplet stationary again.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required.

items.stem: Along a straight dielectric mounting rod inside an evacuated bell jar, two isolated positive sources of charge +12Q and +4Q have separation 4 x, with +12Q at the left end. Observation point P is positioned between them at distance 2 x from +12Q. Using Coulomb constant k, what is the resultant electric field at P expressed in terms of kQ/x²?
items.workedSolution: At P, +12Q produces (12/2²) kQ/x² = 3.00 kQ/x² to the right, while +4Q at distance 2 x produces (4/2²) kQ/x² = 1.00 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 2.00 kQ/x² to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (12/2²) and (4/2²) to obtain 2.00 kQ/x² to the right (D).

items.stem: Along the reference baseline of an electrostatic beam-steering rig, fixed sources q₁ (left, 7 × 10⁻⁹ C) and q₂ (right) lie 1.2 m apart. The electric field vanishes at an interior point 0.4 m to the right of q₁. What is the signed charge q₂?
items.workedSolution: An interior null point requires q₁ and q₂ to have the same sign (+). Equating kq₁/x₀² = kq₂/(d − x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.8 m gives q₂ = q₁((0.8)/(0.4))² = 4.00 × 7 × 10⁻⁹ C = +2.80 × 10⁻⁸ C (B).

markScheme.criterion: Uses q₂ = q₁((d − x₀)/x₀)² with positive sign to obtain +2.80 × 10⁻⁸ C (B).

items.stem: A small test charge is carried along a dashed circular equipotential contour around a fixed point charge. What geometric and energetic property holds everywhere on this path?
items.workedSolution: Since ΔW = qΔV and ΔV = 0 on an equipotential, equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential. Therefore the correct statement is: Everywhere in the field, equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential.

options.distractorRationale: Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles, never parallel.

options.distractorRationale: Any non-orthogonal component of force along an equipotential would do work and change potential.

options.distractorRationale: Radial fields possess concentric spherical equipotentials.

items.stem: An isolated air-spaced sensor capacitor charged to 24.0 V has its gap completely filled with a polar polymer sheet of relative permittivity 3.60. The overlapping plate area is 260 cm², plate separation is 0.900 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 920 pF. (b) 6.67 V. (c) E' = 20.5 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI units in C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d.
Calculates C' = 920 pF.
Recognises isolated Q is constant so V' = V₀ / εᵣ.
Obtains 6.67 V.
Calculates final stored energy E' = 20.5 nJ.
States polar molecules rotate so negative ends face the positive plate.

Explains opposing internal field lowers net field and raises capacitance (polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity).

items.stem: A spacecraft coasts in a perfectly circular orbit around Mars with its engines switched off. Why does its speed remain strictly constant despite Mars continuously pulling on it with a large gravitational force?
items.workedSolution: In circular orbit r is constant, and equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential. Therefore the correct statement is: Its circular orbit lies on a spherical equipotential: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential.

options.label: A
options.text: Its circular orbit lies along a single radial field line where gravitational potential drops linearly.
options.distractorRationale: A circular orbit runs perpendicular to radial field lines, not along them.

options.label: B
options.text: Its engines must secretly cancel gravity because any non-zero force must change kinetic energy.
options.distractorRationale: A force perpendicular to velocity changes direction without changing speed or kinetic energy.

options.label: C
options.text: Gravitational force vanishes at orbital altitude so zero net force acts on the spacecraft.
options.distractorRationale: Gravitational pull provides the centripetal force keeping the spacecraft in orbit.

options.label: D
options.text: Its circular orbit lies on a spherical equipotential: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential

items.stem: Two protons (mass 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge +1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) are separated by 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁰ m in vacuum. Using ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the ratio F_e / F_g of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between them.
items.workedSolution: Since both forces vary as 1/r², r² cancels: F_e / F_g = e² / (4πε₀ G m_p²) = 1.23 × 10³⁶.

markScheme.criterion: Cancels r² to obtain ratio F_e / F_g = 1.23 × 10³⁶.

items.stem: The figure illustrates a parallel-plate capacitor filled with a polar dielectric slab alongside its linear Q–V charging graph.
items.workedSolution: polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity. In the applied electric field between the plates, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity εᵣ. For an isolated capacitor (Q constant), the reduced net field lowers potential difference V = Ed by factor εᵣ, so C = Q/V rises by εᵣ and stored energy E = Q²/(2C) falls by εᵣ (work is done pulling the slab in). If kept connected to a constant-V supply, extra charge flows from the supply so Q and stored energy E = ½CV² both increase by factor εᵣ. During charging from empty at constant emf V, the battery transfers work W = QV, whereas the capacitor stores only the triangular area under the V–Q graph, E = ½QV; the remaining 50% (½QV) is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of the resistance value R.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States that polar dielectric molecules rotate and align with their negative ends facing the positive plate and positive ends facing the negative plate.
L1b: Explains that the aligned dipoles produce an opposing (counter) internal electric field inside the dielectric.
L2a: Explains that the opposing internal field reduces the net electric field E between the plates.
L2b: Deduces for an isolated capacitor (fixed Q) that V = Ed decreases, so C = Q/V increases by factor εᵣ (and E_stored falls by εᵣ).
L3a: Contrasts battery-connected case (fixed V): extra charge flows from the supply so Q and stored energy increase by factor εᵣ.
L3b: Explains that charging at constant V draws W = QV from the battery while storing ½QV (area under V–Q graph), dissipating 50% (½QV) as heat in circuit resistance independent of R.

parts.prompt: Explain microscopically how inserting a polar dielectric increases the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, contrast the effect on V, Q, and stored energy for an isolated versus battery-connected capacitor, and explain why charging a capacitor at constant supply voltage always dissipates 50% of the supplied energy as heat.
parts.expectedAnswer: polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity. In the applied electric field between the plates, polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity εᵣ. For an isolated capacitor (Q constant), the reduced net field lowers potential difference V = Ed by factor εᵣ, so C = Q/V rises by εᵣ and stored energy E = Q²/(2C) falls by εᵣ (work is done pulling the slab in). If kept connected to a constant-V supply, extra charge flows from the supply so Q and stored energy E = ½CV² both increase by factor εᵣ. During charging from empty at constant emf V, the battery transfers work W = QV, whereas the capacitor stores only the triangular area under the V–Q graph, E = ½QV; the remaining 50% (½QV) is dissipated as thermal energy in circuit resistance regardless of the resistance value R.
workingSteps: L1: Polar molecule rotation/alignment (− end to + plate, + end to − plate).
L2: Aligned dipoles create an opposing internal electric field reducing net E between plates.
L3: Isolated (Q fixed → V falls → C = Q/V rises by εᵣ) vs connected (V fixed → extra Q flows) + 50% charging dissipation (½QV vs QV).

items.stem: Equipotential contours separated by equal steps ΔV are mapped around a spherical planet and around an isolated negatively charged sphere −Q.
items.workedSolution: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential. Around both mass M and negative charge −Q, field lines point radially inward and potential is negative (approaching zero at infinity) because work must be done by an external agent to separate a test mass or positive test charge to infinity. In both maps, equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential (ΔW = mΔV or qΔV = 0). Because field strength equals negative potential gradient (−ΔV/Δr), equal-ΔV contours are tightly packed near the surface and spread further apart as 1/r² decreases. However, introducing a negative test charge near −Q reverses the force to repulsion (potential energy becomes positive), whereas gravity always attracts every mass regardless of composition; additionally, electrostatic forces vastly dominate on atomic scales and can be screened by a Faraday cage.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains inward radial field lines and negative potentials around both M and −Q relative to zero at infinity.
L1b: States that external work must be done to move a test mass or positive test charge away from the centre to infinity.
L2a: Explains that equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines everywhere so ΔW = 0 along an equipotential.
L2b: Links increasing separation between equal-ΔV contours with distance to decreasing field strength via E = −ΔV/Δr (and g = −ΔV/Δr).
L3a: Contrasts sign behaviour: replacing +q with −q turns electrostatic force repulsive and makes potential energy positive, whereas gravity is strictly attractive for all masses.
L3b: Notes electrostatic fields are ~10³⁶ times stronger between subatomic particles and can be shielded by conductors, unlike gravity.

parts.prompt: Explain why both field maps share identical inward radial field patterns and negative potentials, explain how equipotential spacing relates to field strength and work done, and discuss key physical differences between the two fields when a positive vs negative test particle is introduced.
parts.expectedAnswer: equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential. Around both mass M and negative charge −Q, field lines point radially inward and potential is negative (approaching zero at infinity) because work must be done by an external agent to separate a test mass or positive test charge to infinity. In both maps, equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines and zero work is done moving a mass or charge along an equipotential (ΔW = mΔV or qΔV = 0). Because field strength equals negative potential gradient (−ΔV/Δr), equal-ΔV contours are tightly packed near the surface and spread further apart as 1/r² decreases. However, introducing a negative test charge near −Q reverses the force to repulsion (potential energy becomes positive), whereas gravity always attracts every mass regardless of composition; additionally, electrostatic forces vastly dominate on atomic scales and can be screened by a Faraday cage.
workingSteps: Explain why both M and −Q have inward field lines and negative potential (zero at infinity).
Link equipotential orthogonality, zero work, and contour spacing to −ΔV/Δr.
Contrast response to opposite test charge sign, force strength ratio, and shielding.

items.stem: Between parallel titanium electrodes inside a beam-diagnostics chamber, across a 0.02 m vacuum gap with potential difference 450 V, a charged silica microsphere carrying +2.5 × 10⁻¹² C and mass 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ kg accelerates from rest from the positive plate to the 0 V plate. Neglecting gravity, what speed does the charged silica microsphere reach upon arriving at the 0 V plate?
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 2.5 × 10⁻¹² × 450 / 5 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 2.12 m s⁻¹ (A).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 2.12 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: Along the symmetry line of a miniature ion-optics bench, collinear charges +4 nC (left) and +16 nC (right) are held at a separation of 0.8 m, while point P is marked 0.5 m from the +4 nC charge. Model the region as vacuum with Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both positive sources repel a positive test charge placed at P, so the left charge pushes rightward while the right charge pushes leftward. (b) |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.5)² = 144 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.3)² = 1.60 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Subtracting the opposing vectors yields 1.45 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: States that a positive test charge between like-sign sources experiences opposite forces from the left and right charges.
Evaluates E = k|q|/r² at r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Subtracts the two opposing field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.45 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.workedSolution: (a) V = k(10 × 10⁻⁹/0.5 + -10 × 10⁻⁹/0.5) = 0 V. (b) At P both fields point to the right, giving E = 360 N C⁻¹ + 360 N C⁻¹ = 719 N C⁻¹ to the right.

Adds the two collinear field magnitudes.
Obtains 719 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.workedSolution: (a) E = (110 − 30) / 0.04 = 2.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right. (b) a = qE / m = 5.00 m s⁻². (c) Using ½mv² = q(80), v = 0.632 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Within a dust-plasma levitation chamber evacuated to low pressure, point charges +7 nC (left) and −2 nC (right) are fixed 0.5 m apart, and point P lies on the line between them 0.3 m from +7 nC. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and define electric potential to be zero at infinity. What is the electric potential at point P?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.2 m. Thus V = 210 V + (−89.9 V) = 120 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.3 + kq₂/0.2 = 120 V (D).

items.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor remains permanently connected across a constant-voltage DC power supply while a polar dielectric slab of relative permittivity εᵣ is inserted between its plates. What happens to the charge and stored energy?
items.workedSolution: At fixed V, C rises by εᵣ so potential difference stays constant so extra charge flows from the supply and stored energy increases by factor relative permittivity. Therefore the correct statement is: While connected to the supply, potential difference stays constant so extra charge flows from the supply and stored energy increases by factor relative permittivity

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: potential difference stays constant so extra charge flows from the supply and stored energy increases by factor relative permittivity.

options.distractorRationale: Ignores that inserting a dielectric multiplies capacitance by εᵣ.

options.text: While connected to the supply, extra charge flows back into the battery so stored energy falls to zero.
options.distractorRationale: Higher capacitance at fixed V requires additional charge from the supply, increasing E = ½CV².

items.stem: Within a dust-plasma levitation chamber evacuated to low pressure, fixed sources carrying +9 nC (on the left) and −3 nC (on the right) have a centre-to-centre separation of 0.8 m. Point P is marked 0.5 m from the +9 nC source along the connecting line. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² throughout.
items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right. (b) With r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.3 m, |E₁| = 324 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 300 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 623 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Explains using a positive test charge that both source fields at P act in the same direction.
Applies E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.5 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Adds the two collinear field magnitudes.

workingSteps: |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 324 N C⁻¹; |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 300 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: Across the test region of a high-impedance electrometer bench, along a 0.6 m axis between −8 nC on the left and −4 nC on the right, a +3 nC probe particle rests momentarily at point P (0.2 m from −8 nC). Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² with the reference of zero potential at infinite separation. What is the electric potential at P due to the two fixed source charges?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.2 + q₂/0.4) = −360 V + (−89.9 V) = −450 V (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.2 + q₂/0.4) = −450 V (B), independent of q_test.

items.stem: Inside a cryogenic linear Paul-trap alignment fixture, fixed sources +7 nC (left) and +5 nC (right) have separation 0.35 m. Observation point P is positioned on the extended axis beyond the right-hand charge, 0.7 m from +7 nC. Model the region as vacuum with Coulomb constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the resultant electric field at exterior point P?
items.workedSolution: Exterior point P is r₁ = 0.7 m to the right of +7 nC and r₂ = 0.7 − 0.35 = 0.35 m to the right of +5 nC. Superposing E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² gives 495 N C⁻¹ to the right (B).

markScheme.criterion: Uses r₁ = 0.7 m and r₂ = 0.35 m to obtain 495 N C⁻¹ to the right (B).

items.stem: Inside a cryogenic linear Paul-trap alignment fixture, isolated point charges +4 nC at x = 0 and +9 nC at x = 0.5 m are mounted along a straight insulating track. At what distance from the +4 nC charge along the line joining the charges is the resultant electric field equal to zero?
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes gives q₁/x² = q₂/(0.5 − x)², so (0.5 − x)/x = √(9/4). Solving yields x = 0.5 × √4/(√4 + √9) = 0.200 m (D).

markScheme.criterion: Equates kq₁/x² = kq₂/(0.5 − x)² to obtain x = 0.200 m (D).

items.stem: In an undergraduate nuclear scattering simulation, a stationary calcium target nucleus (charge +20e) repels an incoming alpha particle (charge +2e) that momentarily comes to rest at separation 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity. What is the electric potential due to the calcium nucleus at distance r_min?
items.workedSolution: Radial potential of the +20e nucleus is V = kZe / r_min = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 20 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.20 × 10⁶ V (A).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = kZe / r_min = 1.20 × 10⁶ V (A).

items.stem: Along the optical axis of a benchtop ion-trap demonstration rig, two fixed positive point charges of +5 nC (left) and +20 nC (right) are held 0.9 m apart. Model the charges in free space (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²), taking V = 0 at infinity. What is the electric potential at the unique point on the line between the charges where the resultant electric field is zero?
items.workedSolution: Zero field occurs at x = 0.9 × √5/(√5 + √20) = 0.300 m from +5 nC (and 0.600 m from +20 nC). Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 450 V (C).

markScheme.criterion: Finds x = 0.300 m and sums positive scalar potentials to obtain 450 V (C).

parts.prompt: Calculate the radius of the droplet in micrometres.
Determine the initial charge on the droplet.
State and explain how the balancing voltage must change if the droplet suddenly loses one excess electron due to ionising radiation.
parts.expectedAnswer: The balancing voltage must increase because losing an electron decreases upward electric force so a greater balancing potential difference is required.
workingSteps: Loss of one electron lowers $|Q|$ from $5e$ to $4e$.
Since $QV/d = mg$ with $mg$ constant, $V$ must rise to restore equilibrium.

items.stem: Within an evacuated spacecraft charge-control test cell, fixed charges +6Q (left) and +27Q (right) sit along an axis in free space separated by 4 x. Point P is marked 1 x to the right of +6Q. Write the resultant electric field magnitude at P in the form E = α kQ/x², where k is the Coulomb constant.
items.workedSolution: (a) The left positive charge produces a larger repulsive field magnitude at P than the right positive charge, so the net electric field points to the right. (b) α = |6/1² − 27/3²| = |6.00 − 3.00| = 3.00.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant direction as to the right with valid reasoning.
Forms inverse-square terms 6/1² and 27/3².
Subtracts the opposing dimensionless field coefficients.
Obtains α = 3.00.

items.stem: Inside an electrostatic aerosol-charging test section, a point charge q₁ = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C sits at x = 0 and an unknown point charge q₂ sits at x = 0.9 m. An axial field scan locates a zero-field null point between them at x = 0.3 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) q₁ and q₂ have the same sign so their fields oppose between them. (b) |q₂/q₁| = ((0.9 − 0.3)/0.3)² = (0.6/0.3)² = 4.00. (c) q₂ = +(4.00)(5 × 10⁻⁹ C) = +2.00 × 10⁻⁸ C.

markScheme.criterion: States same sign because fields must oppose in the region between the charges.
Uses |q₂/q₁| = ((d − x₀)/x₀)² with d − x₀ = 0.6 m.
Obtains 4.00.
Multiplies q₁ by ratio from (b) with positive sign.
Obtains q₂ = +2.00 × 10⁻⁸ C.

items.stem: Equipotential contours separated by equal potential steps ΔV are drawn around a negatively charged sphere. Why are the contours packed closer together near the sphere and wider apart far away?
items.workedSolution: Since E = −ΔV/Δr (and g = −ΔV/Δr), field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field. Therefore the correct statement is: Because field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field.

options.label: A
options.text: Because potential is directly proportional to distance from the centre, making the field stronger far from the charge.
options.distractorRationale: Potential varies as 1/r and field weakens as 1/r² with distance.

options.label: B
options.text: Because field strength equals the negative potential gradient so more closely spaced equipotentials indicate a stronger field

options.label: C
options.text: Because widely spaced equipotentials indicate a steeper potential gradient and a stronger electric field.
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the relation E = −ΔV/Δr: smaller Δr for fixed ΔV means larger |E|.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the contours represent trajectories of stationary test charges accelerating radially outward.
options.distractorRationale: Equipotentials are surfaces of constant potential, not field-line trajectories.

items.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor remains wired across a steady 12.0 V DC power unit while a polar glass dielectric plate (εᵣ = 3.20) slides smoothly to fill the plate separation. The overlapping plate area is 240 cm², plate separation is 0.800 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 850 pF. (b) 10.2 nC. (c) E' = 61.2 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI units in C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d.
Calculates C' = 850 pF.
Recognises supply holds V constant so Q' = C' V₀.
Obtains 10.2 nC.
Calculates final stored energy E' = 61.2 nJ.
States polar molecules rotate so negative ends face the positive plate.

Explains opposing internal field lowers net field and raises capacitance (polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity).

items.stem: Within a medical linear-accelerator pre-injector gap, parallel extraction plates separated by 0.04 m are held at 500 V and 0 V. A stationary proton of mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is released from the 500 V plate. Ignore gravitational and relativistic effects.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E = V / d.
Obtains 1.25 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.
Equates kinetic energy gain to electrical work qV.
Obtains 8.00 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
Rearranges ½mv² = ΔE_k for v = √(2ΔE_k / m).
Obtains 3.10 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Within a dust-plasma levitation chamber evacuated to low pressure, fixed point charges +2 nC (at x = 0) and +10 nC (at x = 0.6 m) occupy a straight insulating rail. Point P is situated at x = 0.4 m. Adopt the free-space constant k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Determine the resultant electric field strength and sense at P.
items.workedSolution: Between like-sign charges, the individual fields at P oppose each other: |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.4)² = 112 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.2)² = 2.25 × 10³ N C⁻¹. Subtracting gives |E_net| = 2.14 × 10³ N C⁻¹ directed to the left (A).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field contributions to obtain 2.14 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (A).

items.stem: Inside a university physics Van de Graaff calibration tunnel, fixed charges −6 nC at x = 0 and +6 nC at x = 0.6 m establish a zero-potential point P on the axis at x = 0.3 m. Model the charges in free space (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²), taking V = 0 at infinity. Although the electric potential at P is zero, what is the resultant electric field at P?
items.workedSolution: Even though V = kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0 at P, the potential gradient dV/dx is non-zero because both opposite charges drive a positive test charge to the left: E = 599 N C⁻¹ + 599 N C⁻¹ = 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (B).

markScheme.criterion: Recognizes E != 0 when V = 0 and sums collinear contributions to obtain 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left (B).

items.stem: Across the planar extraction electrodes of a surface-analysis gun, inside an evacuated cell of gap width 0.03 m biased at 450 V, a charged aerosol particle of mass 3 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge +6 × 10⁻⁹ C travels from the +450 V electrode to the 0 V collector. Neglecting fringing at the plate edges, calculate the uniform electric field strength in the gap.
items.workedSolution: For uniform parallel plates, E = V / d = 450 / 0.03 = 1.50 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A Kelvin-probe scan across a uniform electrostatic region identifies three parallel equipotential lines at 400 V (left), 250 V (middle), and 100 V (right), with adjacent lines spaced 0.03 m apart. A charged dielectric bead of mass 5 × 10⁻⁵ kg and charge +3 × 10⁻⁸ C starts from rest on the middle 250 V line and moves frictionlessly horizontally to the 100 V line. What is the magnitude and direction of the uniform electric field?
items.workedSolution: Electric field points toward decreasing potential (to the right) with magnitude E = |ΔV|/s = (250 − 100) / 0.03 = 5.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (D).

markScheme.criterion: Uses E = −ΔV/Δx to obtain 5.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right (D).

items.stem: Inside a cryogenic linear Paul-trap alignment fixture, point charges +9 nC (left) and −3 nC (right) are fixed 0.6 m apart, and point P lies on the line between them 0.3 m from +9 nC. Assume vacuum (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) and reference all scalar potentials to zero at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) Scalar potential V = k(q₁/0.3 + q₂/0.3) = 180 V. (b) Vector electric field E = 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Applies signed scalar sum V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = 180 V (including sign if negative).
Uses inverse-square magnitudes at r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Combines the two collinear field vectors with proper directions.
Obtains 1.20 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI to find C = 797 pF.

items.stem: On a sapphire isolation substrate inside a cleanroom vacuum stage, two fixed point charges of +8 nC (left) and −4 nC (right) are held 0.6 m apart. Point P lies on the straight line joining them at a distance of 0.4 m to the right of the +8 nC charge. Treat both sources as point charges in vacuum with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Which row gives the magnitude and direction of the electric field vector at P?
items.workedSolution: At P, both opposite-sign sources drive a positive test charge to the right. |E₁| = k|q₁|/r₁² = 449 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/r₂² = 899 N C⁻¹ (with r₂ = 0.2 m). Summing the two same-sense vectors gives E = 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

markScheme.criterion: Adds same-direction inverse-square contributions to obtain 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right (A).

items.stem: Inside an electrostatic aerosol-charging test section, along a 0.9 m axis between −12 nC on the left and +5 nC on the right, a −1.6 nC probe particle rests momentarily at point P (0.4 m from −12 nC). With zero potential set at infinity in vacuum, use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) E = 854 N C⁻¹ to the left. (b) Scalar sum V = k(q₁/0.4 + q₂/0.5) = −180 V. (c) Force on probe F = q_test E = 1.37 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Applies vector superposition E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂².
Obtains 854 N C⁻¹ to the left.
Sums signed scalar potentials k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains −180 V.
Uses F = q_test E with correct sign/direction.
Obtains 1.37 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right.

items.stem: Across the measurement track of a non-contact Kelvin probe bench, two collinear point charges of −6 nC (left) and −3 nC (right) are separated by 0.4 m. Point P lies outside the pair to the right of both charges, at a total distance of 0.7 m from the left-hand −6 nC charge. Use 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² throughout.
items.workedSolution: (a) Because P lies to the right of both like-sign charges, both source fields point to the left and reinforce. (b) Using r₁ = 0.7 m and r₂ = 0.3 m, |E₁| = 110 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 300 N C⁻¹, giving resultant E = 410 N C⁻¹ to the left.

Identifies r₁ = 0.7 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Applies signed vector superposition kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂².
Obtains 410 N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.stem: Across the test region of a high-impedance electrometer bench, isolated point charges +9 nC at x = 0 and +25 nC at x = 0.8 m are mounted along a straight insulating track.
items.workedSolution: (a) Between two positive charges their repulsive fields act in opposite directions, and equal field magnitudes require a smaller distance from the weaker left-hand charge. (b) Setting 9/x² = 25/(0.8 − x)² gives (0.8 − x)/x = √(25/9), hence x = 0.300 m.

markScheme.criterion: Explains opposing fields between positive sources and identifies closer proximity to the left-hand charge.
Equates inverse-square field magnitudes 9/x² = 25/(0.8 − x)².
Takes square roots correctly to linearize for x.
Obtains x = 0.300 m.

parts.prompt: Explain why the resultant electric field can be zero only in the region between the two positive charges and state which charge lies closer to that point.
parts.expectedAnswer: Between two positive charges their repulsive fields act in opposite directions, and equal field magnitudes require a smaller distance from the weaker left-hand charge.
workingSteps: Between two positive charges their repulsive fields act in opposite directions, and equal field magnitudes require a smaller distance from the weaker left-hand charge.

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance from the +9 nC charge to the zero-field point.

items.stem: Along the primary axis of a precision field-mill calibration bench, stationary point charges −7 nC (left) and +7 nC (right) are mounted 0.6 m apart, with axial point P located 0.3 m from the left charge. Take the Coulomb constant as k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.3 m, superposing the two inverse-square fields gives E = 1.40 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left. (b) Using F = q_test E with q_test = −2.2 nC gives F = 3.08 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Uses E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.3 m.
Combines the two collinear field vectors with correct signs.
Obtains 1.40 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.
Multiplies field from (a) by probe charge in coulombs.
Obtains 3.08 × 10⁻⁶ N to the right.

workingSteps: Superpose E_x = kq₁/r₁² + kq₂/r₂² = 1.40 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

parts.prompt: A small test charge of −2.2 nC is now placed at P. Calculate the magnitude and state the direction of the electrostatic force acting on it.
workingSteps: Use F = q_test E with q_test = -2.2 × 10⁻⁹ C.

items.stem: An electrostatic field plotter maps three parallel vertical equipotential surfaces at 180 V (left), 100 V (middle), and 20 V (right), with adjacent lines separated by 0.04 m. A particle of charge +2.5 × 10⁻⁸ C moves from the 180 V line to the 20 V line. What signed work does the electric field do on the charge?
items.workedSolution: Work done by the electric field is W_field = q(V_initial − V_final) = (+2.5 × 10⁻⁸ C)(180 − (20)) = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (B).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates W_field = q(V_i − V_f) = 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ J (B).

items.stem: During a central elastic nuclear encounter in vacuum, a projectile alpha particle of charge +2e approaches head-on a stationary titanium nucleus of atomic number Z = 22 (charge +22e) to a distance of closest approach r_min = 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and zero electric potential at infinity.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = kZe / r_min = 1.22 × 10⁶ V. (b) E_p = 2eV = 3.89 × 10⁻¹³ J. (c) Dividing by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ gives 2.43 × 10⁶ eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Q = 22e and r_min = 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ m into V = kQ/r.
Obtains 1.22 × 10⁶ V.
Multiplies potential from (a) by projectile charge 2e.
Obtains 3.89 × 10⁻¹³ J.
Divides joule energy by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ (or multiplies V in volts by z).
Obtains 2.43 × 10⁶ eV.

Calculate the electrostatic potential energy (in joules) of the alpha particle at closest approach.
Express this electrostatic potential energy in electronvolts (eV).
workingSteps: E_p (in eV) = E_p (in J) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹) = 2.43 × 10⁶ eV.

items.stem: Across the measurement track of a non-contact Kelvin probe bench, stationary charges +16 nC (on the left) and +1 nC (on the right) sit at separation 0.85 m. With zero potential set at infinity in vacuum, use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Setting 16/x² = 1/(0.85 − x)² gives x = 0.680 m. (b) Scalar potentials add: V = k(q₁/x + q₂/(d − x)) = 264 V. (c) By definition of the null point (zero potential gradient), E = 0 N C⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates 16/x² = 1/(0.85 − x)².
Obtains x = 0.680 m.
Adds positive scalar potential contributions kq₁/x + kq₂/(d − x).
Obtains V = 264 V.
States 0 N C⁻¹.

items.stem: What fundamental property of nature did Millikan establish by repeating his oil-drop measurements across hundreds of droplets?
items.workedSolution: Millikan's landmark finding was that all measured droplet charges are integer multiples of the elementary charge proving charge is quantised ($e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$).

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that all measured droplet charges are integer multiples of the elementary charge proving charge is quantised.

options.label: A
options.text: Oil droplets can carry any continuous fractional charge down to arbitrarily small values.
options.distractorRationale: Millikan's data revealed discrete steps of 1.60 × 10^-19 C, disproving continuous charge.

options.label: B
options.text: Gravitational field strength varies linearly with electric field strength between metal plates.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity stayed constant while electric force balanced weight.

options.label: C
options.text: He demonstrated that all measured droplet charges are integer multiples of the elementary charge proving charge is quantised.

options.label: D
options.text: Every oil droplet carries identical mass regardless of atomiser spray conditions.
options.distractorRationale: Droplet radii and masses varied widely; it was charge that appeared in integer steps of e.

items.stem: Within a shielded Faraday enclosure used for sensor testing, positive point charges +6Q (on the left) and +9Q (on the right) are fixed a distance 4 x apart in vacuum. Point P lies on the line joining them at a distance 2 x from +6Q (and 2 x from +9Q). Using Coulomb constant k, what is the resultant electric field at P expressed in terms of kQ/x²?
items.workedSolution: At P, +6Q produces (6/2²) kQ/x² = 1.50 kQ/x² to the right, while +9Q at distance 2 x produces (9/2²) kQ/x² = 2.25 kQ/x² to the left. Net field = 0.750 kQ/x² to the left (C).

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts (6/2²) and (9/2²) to obtain 0.750 kQ/x² to the left (C).

items.stem: Inside a university physics Van de Graaff calibration tunnel, along a 0.6 m vacuum baseline with q₁ = 9 × 10⁻⁹ C at the left end and q₂ at the right end, the net electric field is zero at a point 0.36 m from q₁. What is the magnitude ratio |q₂ / q₁|?
items.workedSolution: At x₀ = 0.36 m, the distance from q₂ is d − x₀ = 0.24 m. Setting |q₁|/x₀² = |q₂|/(d − x₀)² gives |q₂/q₁| = (0.24/0.36)² = 0.444 (C).

items.stem: Which statement accurately compares radial gravitational fields around a spherical mass and radial electric fields around a point charge?
items.workedSolution: Both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential. Therefore the correct statement is: In radial geometry, both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: both obey inverse-square laws with zero potential at infinity, but gravitational force is always attractive with negative potential whereas electric force can attract or repel with positive or negative potential.

options.distractorRationale: Both radial fields follow inverse-square laws (1/r²).

options.label: B
options.text: In radial geometry, gravitational potential is positive near a mass whereas electric potential is always negative near any charge.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the sign of gravitational potential and ignores positive electric potential near +Q.

options.label: C
options.text: In radial geometry, both fields can attract or repel depending on whether the test particle is moving.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity is strictly attractive; static electric forces depend on charge sign, not motion.

items.stem: While permanently connected to a 30.0 V laboratory supply, a parallel-plate capacitor has its air gap filled completely with a polar ceramic dielectric (εᵣ = 5.50). The overlapping plate area is 350 cm², plate separation is 1.50 mm, and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) C' = 1.14e+3 pF. (b) 34.1 nC. (c) E' = 511 nJ. (d) polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity.

markScheme.criterion: Converts cm² and mm to SI units in C = ε₀ εᵣ A / d.
Calculates C' = 1.14e+3 pF.
Recognises supply holds V constant so Q' = C' V₀.
Obtains 34.1 nC.
Calculates final stored energy E' = 511 nJ.
States polar molecules rotate so negative ends face the positive plate.

Explains opposing internal field lowers net field and raises capacitance (polar molecules rotate to align negative ends toward the positive plate, producing an opposing internal electric field that reduces net field and increases capacitance by relative permittivity).

items.stem: Within a medical linear-accelerator pre-injector gap, across a 0.04 m vacuum gap with potential difference 500 V, a proton carrying +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg accelerates from rest from the positive plate to the 0 V plate. Neglecting gravity, what speed does the proton reach upon arriving at the 0 V plate?
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy, ½mv² = qV, so v = √(2qV / m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 / 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷) = 3.10 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (A).

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV to obtain v = 3.10 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: On a low-permittivity PTFE fixture inside an evacuated chamber, along a 0.9 m baseline between fixed charges +10 nC on the left and +4 nC on the right, point P lies 0.3 m from the left source. Assume vacuum permittivity such that k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both positive sources repel a positive test charge placed at P, so the left charge pushes rightward while the right charge pushes leftward. (b) |E₁| = k|q₁|/(0.3)² = 999 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = k|q₂|/(0.6)² = 99.9 N C⁻¹. Subtracting the opposing vectors yields 899 N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: States that a positive test charge between like-sign sources experiences opposite forces from the left and right charges.
Evaluates E = k|q|/r² at r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.6 m.
Subtracts the two opposing field magnitudes.
Obtains 899 N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Along a straight dielectric mounting rod inside an evacuated bell jar, opposite point charges −8 nC (left) and +4 nC (right) are fixed 0.6 m apart. Point P lies on the connecting axis 0.4 m from −8 nC, where the scalar electric potential vanishes. Adopt k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electrostatic potential at infinite distance.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = k(-8 × 10⁻⁹/0.4 + 4 × 10⁻⁹/0.2) = 0 V. (b) At P both fields point to the left, giving E = 449 N C⁻¹ + 899 N C⁻¹ = 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes signed charges with r₁ = 0.4 m and r₂ = 0.2 m into V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂).
Obtains V = 0 V.
Applies inverse-square law E = k|q|/r² to both sources.
Adds the two collinear field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.35 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the left.

items.stem: Inside an electrostatic ink-droplet test nozzle in vacuum, inside an evacuated cell of gap width 0.08 m biased at 800 V, a charged aerosol particle of mass 6 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge +2 × 10⁻⁸ C travels from the +800 V electrode to the 0 V collector. Neglect edge effects and gravitational forces.
items.workedSolution: (a) Uniform field E = V / d = 800 / 0.08 = 1.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. (b) Work done by the field W = qV = (2 × 10⁻⁸)(800) = 1.60 × 10⁻⁵ J.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes V = 800 V and d = 0.08 m into E = V / d.
Obtains 1.00 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Obtains 1.60 × 10⁻⁵ J.

items.stem: An electrostatic field plotter maps three parallel vertical equipotential surfaces at 540 V (left), 320 V (middle), and 100 V (right), with adjacent lines spaced 0.055 m apart. A Millikan oil micro-droplet of mass 6.4 × 10⁻¹³ kg and charge +3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ C starts from rest on the middle 320 V line and moves frictionlessly horizontally to the 100 V line.
items.workedSolution: (a) E = (320 − 100) / 0.055 = 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right. (b) a = qE / m = 20.0 m s⁻². (c) Using ½mv² = q(220), v = 1.48 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides adjacent potential step by spacing s.
Obtains 4.00 × 10³ V m⁻¹ to the right.
Applies a = qE / m.
Obtains 20.0 m s⁻².
Equates ½mv² = q(220) or uses v² = 2as.
Obtains 1.48 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Inside a university physics Van de Graaff calibration tunnel, point charges +12 nC (left) and −5 nC (right) are fixed 0.8 m apart, and point P lies on the line between them 0.3 m from +12 nC. Adopt k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and zero electrostatic potential at infinite distance. What is the electric potential at point P?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential is a signed scalar: V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂) with r₁ = 0.3 m and r₂ = 0.5 m. Thus V = 360 V + (−89.9 V) = 270 V (B).

markScheme.criterion: Sums signed scalar potentials kq₁/0.3 + kq₂/0.5 = 270 V (B).

items.stem: An air-filled capacitor (area 400 cm², gap 1.00 mm, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹) is charged to 40.0 V and then disconnected. A dielectric slab with εᵣ = 4.00 is inserted to fill the gap. Calculate the final electrical energy stored in nanojoules.
items.workedSolution: C₀ = 354 pF, E₀ = ½C₀V₀² = 283 nJ. Isolated Q fixed ⇒ E' = E₀ / εᵣ = 70.8 nJ.

markScheme.criterion: Finds isolated final energy 70.8 nJ.

items.stem: Inside an electrostatic aerosol-charging test section, charges +3.5 nC and −7 nC are separated horizontally by 0.7 m, with +3.5 nC on the left. Observation point P is situated between them, 0.2 m from the left-hand source. Take the Coulomb constant as k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Both individual electric field vectors at P point to the right (away from the positive left source and toward the negative right source), so they reinforce toward the right. (b) With r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.5 m, |E₁| = 787 N C⁻¹ and |E₂| = 252 N C⁻¹. Summing gives 1.04 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

markScheme.criterion: Explains using a positive test charge that both source fields at P act in the same direction.
Applies E = k|q|/r² with r₁ = 0.2 m and r₂ = 0.5 m.
Adds the two collinear field magnitudes.
Obtains 1.04 × 10³ N C⁻¹ to the right.

items.stem: Along a straight dielectric mounting rod inside an evacuated bell jar, along a 0.6 m axis between −4 nC on the left and +10 nC on the right, a −2.5 nC probe particle rests momentarily at point P (0.4 m from −4 nC). With zero potential set at infinity in vacuum, use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the electric potential at P due to the two fixed source charges?
items.workedSolution: Electric potential at P depends only on the source charges: V = k(q₁/0.4 + q₂/0.2) = −89.9 V + (450 V) = 360 V (D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates V = k(q₁/0.4 + q₂/0.2) = 360 V (D), independent of q_test.
